doc.title: Ray Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Record dates: 'Primrose Lane', 'The Big Hurt' and Capitol work
summary: He recalls his hits, the Radio Recorders filter effect, rock and rhythm and blues calls, and 'Li'l Abner' with Nelson Riddle.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Can you recall some of the records you played on?
Well I think the only hit I was on was something Lane — “Primrose Lane.” And I think I faked an introduction on that, and they always say evidently whatever I did was good.

Yeah. Because I did a record date after that, it was funny, a friend of mine, Jack Marshall, the guitar player, it was one of his dates. And he came over to me and he said, “do you think you could play something like the guy played on the ‘Primrose Lane’ intro?”
But I didn’t realize that that was considered an important part of the record.
But I think there was another one: “The Big Hurt” does that ring a bell?
It sounds like something from one of the vocal groups.
It was a solo singer, a female singer, the other was a male singer. And you know you could look them up and they’re probably on some list. And that had a gimmick, Radio

Recorders got to be a famous place I guess, a recording studio. This was when they were kind of making the records. And the guy owned it you know, and he was the engineer, and he had this thing, he had some kind of filter that he’d put — it got a very strange sound if you ever hear it, there was an effect on it that he used.
On the whole record or just the piano?
There’s a name for it. Yeah, I think it went through the whole record, a very ethereal kind of effect.

Yeah one of those kind of things, that’s right, exactly. There’s a name for it, I’ve forgot what they call it. Like a filter that changes pitches and goes up and down the spectrum, kind of like that. Oh the gal sang good, she had good musicians, pretty good tune, for a pop tune. So I did a lot of them. As I say most of them weren’t hits. But I got through it. They probably sold. For Capitol I think mostly I worked. And then I started getting movie calls. I remember working with Nelson Riddle on “L’il Abner” which may have been one of the — that’s one story that I remember, it was one of the early calls I got. And it seemed like I kind of got in the pool, you know like the contractors have lists of people, and you get on their list and you start getting like two, three calls a week or something.
